cues.text: A Mediterranean Under Threat

By 1570, the Ottoman Empire , having already taken Cyprus from Venice, controlled the eastern Mediterranean so thoroughly that the coasts of Italy and Spain themselves lay within realistic reach of Ottoman naval power.
Pope St. Pius V , recognizing the scale of the danger, spent months in difficult diplomacy.
He persuaded Spain, Venice, the Papal States, and several smaller Italian powers to set aside their considerable mutual rivalries and unite in a single defensive alliance.
Venice in particular had already lost the strategically vital island of Cyprus to Ottoman forces the previous year.
Reports of the brutal treatment inflicted on the island's defenders after its surrender lent the coming confrontation an urgency beyond ordinary territorial calculation.
The Holy League
The resulting Holy League , formed in the spring of 1571, assembled a combined fleet of roughly two hundred ships.
It placed this fleet under the command of the twenty-four-year-old Don John of Austria , illegitimate half-brother of King Philip II of Spain.
He was a young, largely untested commander tasked with holding together a coalition whose constituent powers, particularly Venice and Spain, had barely trusted one another even in forming it.
A Spiritual as Well as Naval Preparation
Pius V was convinced that the coming battle was a spiritual struggle as much as a military one.

He urged Catholics across Europe to pray the Rosary for the fleet's success, ordered churches kept open day and night for prayer, and had every ship in the Holy League's fleet blessed before it sailed.
Aboard the vessels themselves, chaplains distributed rosaries to the assembled crews, and on the eve of battle the men of the fleet knelt on their own decks to pray them together.
The Battle in the Gulf of Patras
On October 7, 1571, the Holy League's fleet met the Ottoman navy in the Gulf of Patras, near the town of Lepanto.
Despite facing a fleet of comparable or greater size, the Christian forces — aided by innovative Venetian galleasses mounting broadside cannon — won a decisive and bloody victory.
Ottoman commander Ali Pasha was killed in the fighting, while some 25,000 Ottoman sailors and soldiers were killed or captured.
The bulk of the Ottoman fleet was destroyed or taken, at a cost of roughly 7,500 Christian dead.
The admiral of the Genoese contingent, Andrea Doria, is remembered as having carried an image of Our Lady of Guadalupe aboard his own flagship throughout the engagement.
This was one of many small devotional gestures woven through a fleet whose crews had been assured repeatedly, in the days before battle, that they fought under Our Lady's own particular protection.
A Vision in Rome
Tradition holds that Pius V, meeting with his cardinals in Rome on the very afternoon of the battle, suddenly rose and went to a window.

He declared that the Christian fleet had at that moment won a great victory — a claim confirmed only some two weeks later, when the first official word of the battle finally reached Rome by conventional courier.

Whatever the precise circumstances of the pope's own knowledge, he attributed the victory unhesitatingly to the intercession of the Blessed Virgin, invoked through the Rosary he had asked all Christendom to pray.
Legacy
In thanksgiving, Pius V instituted an annual feast of Our Lady of Victory .
Pope Gregory XIII renamed it the Feast of the Holy Rosary two years later.
Pope Clement XI extended it to the universal Church in 1716, establishing the origin of the feast still kept every October 7.
Lepanto did not end the Ottoman naval threat outright, but it broke the empire's aura of invincibility at sea.

It halted the empire's westward advance into the central Mediterranean for good, remaining, in Catholic memory, the paradigm case of a decisive military outcome the Church has always attributed, first and above every tactical explanation, to the power of prayer.
